title: Hypertrophy Q&A #3
summary: Third hypertrophy Q&A covering squat pauses, body-part prioritization, exercise hierarchies and rotations, tonnage tracking, loaded carries, rear/side delt progression, athletic work, Olympic lifting and back development, cardio, drop sets, deadlift negatives. Ends with a long rebuttal of HIT/one-set-to-failure training.
claims: If you can only squat with a pause at the bottom, you likely lack balance and the strength to reverse out of the hole without your torso tipping into a good-morning
Torso angle should be the same on the way down and the way up in a squat; if it changes, the bottom-position strength needs training
The pause squat is meant as a harder variation to help the back squat progress; if it is your only squat you lack a main mover and will plateau
Going far below parallel puts more stress on the lumbar spine and posterior chain
The idea that shortened range is best for the quads is a myth; quads are also stretched below parallel
Squatting to parallel or a hair below is fine because the heavier load you can move (e.g. 60 lb more than paused) drives more progression
Parallel depth gives you a gauge to keep every rep consistent; quarter squats stress the knees with no benefit
Learn to reverse the negative into the positive with a controlled bounce, practicing with light weight (e.g. 50 lb) and adding load
Specializing a body part for one month does little; the muscle needs several months to acclimate to higher volume before it pays off
Only specialize a body part for a serious reason (a weak point or a strong desire) and be patient
He has been neglecting his quads and biceps while prioritizing weaker body parts like triceps for over a year and plans to continue
Rotating month-long priorities makes the previous priority regress; prefer raising tonnage on all muscles while sandbagging some and fast-tracking others
Fast-tracked muscles still need adaptation phases because tendons and muscle can't absorb immense jumps at once
Within an exercise hierarchy (main, accessory, extra) you can go to 4-6 movements as long as specificity is respected
Having both bench and dips as top-level horizontal presses creates too much variation for most; pick one as king unless you're a hyper-specialist
People who have the shoulders and rib cage for dips should do dips; dips and bench are each well complemented by push-ups
You could alternate dips one week and bench the next, letting each develop on its own while the muscles carry over
About 85% of the lifts in his current program were there when he created it; he rarely replaces anything
A rotation is a temporary substitution, not a replacement; a lift must be practiced every 10-12 days or it doesn't belong in the program
Low-technicality hinges like good mornings and RDLs can be practiced less strictly; main lifts like squat and deadlift need regular practice
A typical hierarchy: bench, then close-grip bench, then a fly for the pump; hierarchies are also horizontal (spoto press alongside close-grip, push-ups alongside flies)
Don't change programs until your body forces you to; watch for repeated small plateaus on the same part of the program as a sign of a big plateau
You can stay on linear progression in bodybuilding, but it requires a non-minimalist program with days that feed each other, e.g. week A/week B rotations
Every progression method is valid; how you program around it makes or breaks it
Tonnage stability is relative; don't add sets just to hit a tonnage number, because set and rep progress should dictate tonnage, not the reverse
When two main lifts jump the same week, causing a tonnage spike, sandbag one (same weight and reps, work on technique or tempo) and prioritize the other
He himself sandbags either squat or deadlift when both go up in the same week
Tonnage calculations are most useful when progress stalls, to pinpoint where the leak or plateau comes from; don't obsess over them
Loaded carries are excellent for traps, shoulders, upper back and forearms because they are a weighted stretch
Weighted stretch drives muscle fiber damage; it is essentially the negative
Farmer walks can be programmed as strength work, GPP or their own day
He can't do farmer walks because of eight months of frozen weather and no garage space
Sandbag carries with elbows high train thoracic extension like a front squat; they load less, so they lean toward GPP while farmer walks lean toward strength
He likes 4-8 reps on bench because of capricious shoulders; many go too low in volume on bench variations
Suggested ranges: 6-10 on paused bench, 8-12 on spoto press; his favorite is close-grip bench 4x6-10, which progressed extremely fast
He isolates rear and side delts only with dumbbells; face pulls, Arnold raises and Meadows raises work best for him; overhead press mainly grows his front delt
Don't ego lift small muscles; add 5 lb total (2.5 per hand) and stay in 6-12 or 8-12 reps, never below 6
Progress rear delt frequency gradually: 1x/week 3 sets, then 2x/week 6 sets, then 2x4, eventually 3x/week 4 sets
He is not athletic and hasn't run in a year; when he trained for athleticism he never combined it with squats or deadlifts
Program sprints like deadlifts: intense, well warmed up, once or twice a week, and as far from heavy squat/deadlift days as possible
You can't be maximally big and maximally athletic; at some point you must choose
Favorite athletic-hypertrophy crossover moves: high pulls with full triple extension, sprints, swimming, push-ups and pull-ups
He does pull-ups every day for 40-60 reps
Cleans and snatches are pulls from the floor and count as deadlift variations; when he says deadlift he means the conventional deadlift
Chinese weightlifters deadlift all the time and Russians use snatch-grip deadlifts
Pulls from the floor do nothing for back width; width comes from rear delts and lats via vertical and horizontal pulls that involve elbow flexion
His back had zero width when he only deadlifted; it was thick but not wide
Deadlifts mainly build hamstrings, glutes, erectors, rhomboids and mid/lower traps; upper traps come more from partials
Explosive movements still build muscle because they accumulate and progress tonnage
Deadlift progress feeds every other hinge; carryover to the squat is real but weaker than people think
Cardio doesn't cannibalize muscle; it uses calories that should fuel recovery, so it kills gains indirectly
Drop sets and rest-pause are fine tools for accumulating tonnage but shouldn't be applied to strength work or main lifts
Deadlift negatives are riskier because you are fatigued and the weight pulls you, so any form fault from the concentric becomes an injury on the way down
Most RDLs done for low reps are really partials stopping at the kneecap; a true RDL goes until the plates are close to the floor without bouncing
Controlling the deadlift negative does give more hypertrophy, but the concentric-only puller will out-rep, out-progress and get injured less
The limiting factor of every hinge is the concentric; train the positive with heavy deadlifts and the negative with RDLs and hyperextensions
HIT is a cult; HIT followers don't realize he also trains at high intensity, just across many sets
100% intensity is the max; forced reps and partner help only shift the intensity window, they don't exceed 100%
Two reps at 90% beat one rep at 110%; intense tonnage doesn't make up for lack of volume, since volume and intensity go hand in hand
HIT preachers don't show their bodies; Dorian and Mentzer were on steroids so their methods aren't relevant to naturals
One-set trainees are lazy; multiplying sets is harder than one hard set, and intensity is a number, not a sensation
Failure means you cannot do another rep; there's no such thing as absolute or partial failure
With six hard sets he can modulate his training; with one set, if it stops progressing you have nothing left
If one set kept producing linear progress, HIT trainees would squat 1000 lb; forced negatives and constant lift rotation camouflage a lack of progression
As you advance you must lengthen sessions because you run out of room to progress; not wanting to train beyond 25 minutes questions your love for the iron
Set multiplication is muscular endurance: the ability to return to baseline and move relevant weight again
Don't care about aerobic vs anaerobic; just use a wide variety of rep ranges
Hard sets needed to progress depend on level: from 3 to 9 to 12 a week; more advanced lifters need more sets
After one all-out set you could still get ~80% of the reps, so intensity was not used up; you must keep working until you can't return to baseline
One set to failure barely touches maximum recoverable volume, which is a resource targeted through set accumulation
Overtraining is a myth; doing more than the minimum to stimulate growth is just training, and advanced bodies tolerate more tonnage
